title: How do you compare your portfolio to the S&P 500?
summary: Use a time-weighted return, the same dates and a total-return yardstick, and add other benchmarks if you own more than large US stocks.
body_markdown:
## How do you calculate your portfolio’s return?


The number your app shows as “return” may not be the one you want. There are two common methods, and they answer different questions.


A time-weighted return measures how your investments did, with the effect of deposits and withdrawals removed. It’s the right number to set next to an index, because the index never gets a new deposit. The CFA Institute’s performance standards (GIPS) require firms to present time-weighted returns for most portfolios for this reason.


A money-weighted return, sometimes called your personal rate of return, includes the timing of your own cash flows. If you added a lot of money just before a rally, it will look better than the time-weighted number, and the reverse if you added before a drop. It answers “how did my money do,” not “how did my investments do.”


Brokerages don’t all use the same method. Fidelity says your Personal Rate of Return uses a money-weighted formula that reflects the size and timing of your trades. Robinhood says deposits and transfers are left out of its portfolio return, using a method based on the Modified Dietz formula. The quickest check is your broker’s help page on returns.


A simple change in your balance is the least useful number of all. If you started the year at $50,000, added $10,000 and ended at $66,000, the balance rose 32%, but much of that was your own deposit.
